data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The fetch budget should be denominated in bytes only, as bytes directly measure the information transfer cost; exhaustion must be recorded as a typed terminal with a byte counter and a causal link to the budget policy, ensuring replayability through deterministic byte accounting.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If per-request overhead (e.g., TLS handshake, connection setup) dominates cost, a byte budget may allow an unbounded number of requests, leading to denial-of-service or cost surprises.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent can request compressed vs. uncompressed responses, byte counting becomes ambiguous unless the counting rule is fixed and environment-independent.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the environment introduces variable metadata sizes that are not captured by a simple byte count, the budget may be inconsistent across replays.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Bytes are the fundamental resource consumed in network I/O. A byte budget sets a cap B. The agent sums the byte length of each response body (or a deterministic function thereof) and halts when the cumulative sum reaches B. The terminal state records the final byte count, the cap, and the sequence of response sizes. Because response sizes are determined by the environment and the agent's requests (which are part of the replayable policy), the byte counter is deterministic across replays. This prevents silent degradation by making the budget a hard physical limit that cannot be exceeded without triggering a visible, auditable stop.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
